### The Library of Unfinished Things

There should be a library for unfinished things.

Not a library of books that were never completed, though those would deserve a shelf of their own: novels abandoned in chapter seven, memoirs stopped halfway through a difficult childhood, grand histories that dissolve into notes about weather. This library would be broader. It would hold every project, promise, plan, and thought that began with energy and then quietly slipped out of the world.

Inside, there would be a room for languages people meant to learn. On the shelves would sit Italian workbooks with the first three chapters carefully completed, Japanese flashcards arranged by color, dictionaries with train tickets pressed between the pages. There would be notebooks containing lists of useful phrases: “Where is the station?” “How much does this cost?” “I would like coffee.” Most of them would stop there, at the threshold of usefulness, just before the strange and beautiful complexity of speaking to another person.

Another room would contain musical instruments. Guitars with their strings slightly dusty. A violin whose case still smells like resin. Keyboards bought during January, when the year is young and everyone believes they are capable of becoming someone new. Beside each instrument would be the sheet music of songs learned only as far as the chorus. The library would not mock these efforts. It would understand that the first chorus is often the hardest part: the part in which a person has to face the gap between what they admire and what their hands can actually do.

There would be shelves for letters never sent.

Some would be angry letters, written late at night and folded in half by morning. Some would be apologies that arrived too late to feel safe. Some would be love letters written by people who were not sure whether love was a door opening or a floor disappearing beneath them. There would be messages typed into glowing phone screens and then deleted, sentences composed in the shower, speeches imagined during long walks home.

“Here is what I should have said,” each one would begin.

The library would preserve them all.

In one quiet wing, there would be plans for gardens. Not gardens that failed, exactly, but gardens that existed in imagination with greater clarity than they ever did in soil. There would be sketches of raised beds, lists of herbs, measurements of balconies, drawings of small stone paths that curve toward benches under climbing roses. A person might visit this room and find the garden they planned during a winter when their apartment felt too small. They might see that they had wanted mint, tomatoes, lavender, and one tiny lemon tree. Perhaps they had wanted the garden not because they loved gardening, but because they wanted evidence that life could be tended.

The library’s most crowded hall would probably be the Hall of Future Selves.

This room would contain the versions of people they had intended to become. The runner who wakes at dawn. The person who keeps their finances organized. The friend who remembers every birthday. The traveler who owns one good backpack and knows how to move through unfamiliar airports without fear. The reader who finishes difficult books. The cook who never lets vegetables rot in the bottom drawer of the refrigerator.

Each future self would have its own label, its own carefully written description.

“More disciplined.”

“Less afraid.”

“Healthier.”

“Someone who calls home.”

Visitors might wander through this hall feeling ashamed at first. It is easy to feel ashamed around unfinished ambitions. They can seem like evidence in a case against us, proof that we are less determined, less gifted, or less serious than we claimed to be.

But perhaps the librarian would correct this misunderstanding.

“Unfinished does not mean false,” they would say.

That would be the library’s central principle. An unfinished thing was still real. The half-written poem existed. The abandoned painting existed. The friendship that faded without a final argument still existed. The promise to learn how to bake bread was not erased simply because the flour expired in the cupboard.

We tend to believe that only completed things count. Finished books are placed on shelves. Graduates receive diplomas. Buildings are photographed after the scaffolding comes down. A marathon has a finish line, a wedding has a ceremony, a meal ends with empty plates. Completion makes things easy to recognize. It gives them an edge, a shape, a date.

But much of life has no clean ending.

A friendship may become less frequent without becoming less meaningful. A dream may change form without disappearing. A person may spend years trying to understand something and never arrive at an answer. Some of the most important work we do is unfinished by nature: forgiving someone, raising a child, recovering from grief, learning how to live with ourselves.

The Library of Unfinished Things would know this.

It would not arrange its collection by failure. It would arrange it by tenderness.

There would be a small reading room for abandoned hobbies, filled with origami cranes that never became a thousand, knitting projects that stopped halfway down one sleeve, astronomy guides with constellations traced in pencil, chess books marked with coffee rings. A visitor could sit at a table beneath a green lamp and look through their former enthusiasms. They might remember that, for three weeks one summer, they were fascinated by calligraphy. For a month, they watched documentaries about beekeeping. For years, they believed they would someday build a small wooden boat.

Maybe they never did. Maybe they still will.

Time in this library would behave differently. A project abandoned ten years ago would not necessarily be dead. It might simply be waiting in storage, like a seed in a paper envelope. The visitor could take it down from the shelf and examine it again. Some things would feel too distant, too connected to a former self. Others might suddenly spark with unexpected warmth.

“Oh,” someone might say, holding an old notebook. “I still care about this.”

That sentence alone could change a life.

Of course, not every unfinished thing should be resumed. Some plans are left behind because they belonged to a version of us that no longer exists. Some relationships end because they need to. Some ambitions become cages when we insist on carrying them long after they have stopped offering light.

The library would not pressure anyone to check out their old dreams.

It would simply keep them safe.

There is mercy in that. There is mercy in knowing that the person you were trying to become has not vanished entirely, even if you no longer wish to become them. They remain part of your history, evidence of what you once hoped for. Hope is not embarrassing just because it was temporary.

Near the exit, there would be a desk where visitors could donate new items. People would arrive carrying unfinished screenplays, unused gym memberships, business ideas scribbled on napkins, recipes copied from grandparents, unfinished degree applications, maps of trips postponed for reasons both practical and mysterious.

The librarian would accept each offering without judgment.

“Would you like it catalogued under ‘someday,’ ‘almost,’ or ‘not yet’?” they would ask.

And sometimes, after a long pause, a visitor would hold the item a little closer and say, “Actually, I think I’ll take this one back.”

Then they would leave the library carrying a small, unfinished thing into the afternoon, where the world—messy, incomplete, and still in progress—would be waiting.
